transcript: Meeting header: 2027-02-03 16:00 UTC | Duration 52m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Luis Ramirez (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Zenith Head of AI), Tom Reynolds (Zenith Platform), Priya Singh (Zenith Security)
Summary: Demo of Redwood structured output (JSON mode), function/tool calling, Console guardrails; discuss POC scope and security requirements
Topics: structured-output schemas, JSON mode, function-calling vs tool-calling, guardrails, Console observability, POC benchmarks, security (SOC2/SAML/KMS/VPC)
[00:00] Jamie Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh quick intros, I'm Jamie, I'm the AE for your account, with Luis who will run through the demo. Aisha?
[00:12] Aisha Khan: Hi, yeah thanks. I'm Aisha, head of AI at Zenith. We're evaluating structured output for a handful of internal tools and a customer-facing assistant.

[00:25] Luis Ramirez: great, thanks Aisha. Quick agenda: show API JSON mode + schemas, then Console demo of guardrails and per-route settings, then Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization and then Q&A and next steps.
[00:40] Tom Reynolds: quick note, security will join on questions, that's Priya - she'll ask about VPC and KMS specifics later.

[01:10] Luis Ramirez: cool, jumping in. First demo — API call in JSON mode. We'll show a prompt that asks the model to output a purchase_order JSON: fields order_id, items[], total_usd, customer: {id, name} and we provide a JSON schema to enforce types.

[02:00] Luis Ramirez: Showing code: POST /v1/generate with "structured_output": "json" and "schema": <schema blob>. We're using Redwood-hosted endpoint in this demo but the same applies to Dedicated / Private setups.
[02:22] Aisha Khan: are you validating on the service side or is it just a prompt engineering thing?

[02:35] Luis Ramirez: good question — Redwood has two layers: 1) model-side enforcement where we pass the schema as a strong hint in JSON mode and 2) Console/edge guardrails that validate the response and either reject or auto-repair via function-calling. So you get deterministic schemas enforced at the router level.

[03:10] Jamie Park: quick practical note, if you need strict guarantees we can run the POC on Dedicated or Private to control drift and lineage, but hosted still gives schema validation and automatic fallbacks.
[03:45] Priya Singh: for compliance we need audit logs and KMS integration. We're SOC 2 in flight and SAML ok; do you support HSM-backed keys?

[04:05] Luis Ramirez: yes, we integrate with customer KMS and HSM options in Private, and we emit per-request audit logs to your log sink; Console shows token-level attribution. We can include SOC 2 and our security pack doc in the follow-up.
[04:45] Tom Reynolds: can you demo a failure mode — like model returns a string where schema expects number — what happens?

[05:05] Luis Ramirez: sure, I'll run an example where the model returns total_usd as "one twenty". Watch Console: Router applies schema check, flags the response, and triggers the configured policy. Our default policy is to attempt auto-correction via a function call that parses and re-emits valid JSON; alternatively you can choose to reject the response and return an error code to the caller.

[06:12] [screen share] Luis: running demo... (typing) ... model returned malformed total_usd, Console shows validation failure, reenqueued a function-calling repair step, patch applied, final output returned as valid JSON — you can see the event in the trace and the corrected payload in the audit log.
[07:00] Aisha Khan: oh nice — so the function-calling is something Redwood orchestrates or we write the function?

[07:12] Luis Ramirez: Redwood supports both. You can register tool endpoints/functions in Console, and the runtime will call them (tool-calling) to repair or enrich outputs, or you can embed repair logic client-side. We also support automatic small helper functions for simple parsing/validation.

[07:45] Jamie Park: this is where guardrails and rate limits matter — if a failing model causes repeated retries you want smart backoff; Console has per-route retry and fallback settings which we showed earlier in the deck.
[08:20] Tom Reynolds: switching topics — latency/cost tradeoff. For our high-throughput batch jobs we care about throughput > low latency. What do you recommend?

[08:35] Luis Ramirez: for throughput jobs use Redwood Dedicated with continuous batching and our batch-friendly kernels; Optimize will recommend batching windows, KV cache use for prefixes and quantization profile for your workload. For low-latency interactive agents keep Hosted or Dedicated tuned for small-batch immediate responses.
[09:10] Aisha Khan: can Optimize produce config suggestions automatically?

[09:18] Luis Ramirez: yes, Optimize analyzes traces and token distributions and surfaces suggestions: batch size, cache TTLs, quantization levels, and model variants. It also shows estimated cost delta if you change settings — helpful for tradeoffs.

[10:05] [12:30] Luis Ramirez: back to structured output, here's an example of function-calling where the model emits a call payload: "call: create_order, args: {...}". Redwood maps that to a registered tool URL and invokes it with a signed request; the result is instrumented and appears in Console traces.
[11:00] Priya Singh: signed requests — is that mutual TLS or token-based?
[11:12] Luis Ramirez: we support mTLS for Private and token-based with short-lived signatures for Hosted/Dedicated. All calls can be routed through your VPC egress for e2e control.
[12:00] Aisha Khan: what's the typical failure rate for auto-repair, like how often does the function-calling fix it vs manual intervention?

[12:18] Luis Ramirez: varies by schema complexity; for simple type fixes and missing fields repair success is high (80-95%). For more complex semantic mismatches you might need a hybrid approach — sample-based tests in Console evals help catch those pre-prod.

[13:00] [15:00] Luis Ramirez: demo of Console route settings: per-model timeout, token limit, schema enforcement level (soft vs hard), fallback routing to cheaper model variant. Also showing token-level cost breakdown and a per-prompt trace.
[14:10] Tom Reynolds: can we pin model versions for compliance and A/B testing?
[14:22] Jamie Park: yes pinning and rollout policies (canary/A-B) are supported, with automatic fallback; Console stores model version metadata and rollout history for audits.
[15:00] Aisha Khan: curious about data retention and logs, what's the expiration and can we send to our SIEM?

[15:18] Luis Ramirez: retention is configurable for Private and Dedicated; Hosted has default retention but we offer log export to your S3 or SIEM. We'll include the retention matrix in the security pack.

[16:10] [18:00] Luis Ramirez: switching back to function/tool-calling: here's a live example where the model identifies a user intent to book a meeting and returns a structured booking object; Redwood then calls a registered calendar-tool endpoint which returns success/failure and the system returns a final JSON response to the client.
[17:05] Aisha Khan: are these calls idempotent and logged so we can replay for debugging?
[17:20] Luis Ramirez: yes we include request IDs and event logs; Console traces let you replay the exact sequence and payloads for debugging (with PII redaction controls).
[18:45] Tom Reynolds: question about cost — what are the main levers we should look at in the POC?

[19:00] Luis Ramirez: main levers: model choice (size), quantization profile, batching windows, prefix caching for repeated prompts, and choice of Dedicated reserved capacity vs pay-as-you-go hosted. Optimize will recommend expected cost improvements per lever.

[19:40] Jamie Park: for the POC we usually run a short benchmark with a representative prompt set and traffic pattern; Luis will share the benchmark spreadsheet so you can see estimated QPS, latency, and cost under different configs.

[20:15] [22:00] Luis Ramirez: demo — showing schema-driven tests in Console Evals: you upload prompt set, expected structured outputs, and we run regression checks across model versions. You can set alerts for quality regressions tied to eval thresholds.
[21:10] Priya Singh: for compliance we need eval logs and the ability to freeze model versions during audits — is that possible?
[21:26] Jamie Park: yes, you can freeze a rollout and we persist eval snapshots; we'll include details in the POC runbook.
[22:40] Aisha Khan: any gotchas on the schema side? e.g., nested arrays or highly polymorphic fields?

[22:55] Luis Ramirez: complex polymorphic structures are harder to guarantee; best practice is to keep schemas explicit and small, or emit a discriminant field so the router can validate against specific subschemas. We can also use a hybrid approach of returning a top-level type and then a second call to fetch the details.
[23:30] Tom Reynolds: can Redwood integrate with our internal feature store if we want to enrich outputs?
[23:45] Luis Ramirez: yes via tool endpoints — instrumented calls can reach your feature store behind your VPC; the runtime will include short-lived signed tokens.

[24:30] [26:00] Luis Ramirez: walking through a POC plan: 2 weeks bench + 2 weeks integration. Goals: validate schema correctness, latency/cost, and security posture. Deliverables: benchmark report, config suggestions from Optimize, and a recorded runbook for production rollout.
[25:10] Aisha Khan: internal timeline — we're aiming to decide by end of Q1, POC would need to start next week ideally.
[26:40] Jamie Park: that's doable. We'll aim to start week of 2027-02-14. I'll send a POC outline and sign-up sheet after this call.
[27:30] Priya Singh: a couple of security items: can you share your SOC 2 report, pen-test summary, and a red-team note? Also need architecture diagram for Private deployment.
[28:00] Jamie Park: yes, we'll attach the security pack and Private deployment diagram in the follow-up. Luis will include the integration notes for KMS and mTLS.

[29:10] [31:00] Luis Ramirez: quick re-demo of auto-repair flow: model mis-typed date format, function called, console repaired to ISO date, you can see the event sequence and the cost for the extra call highlighted in the trace.
[30:20] Tom Reynolds: cost of auto-repair — is that billed as extra token cost or as a separate function call cost?
[30:35] Luis Ramirez: both: model re-generation is billed as additional tokens and tool-call egress is accounted for in the overall request cost. Console's cost breakdown shows these line items.
[31:50] Aisha Khan: how do we test for regression when model versions change?
[32:05] Luis Ramirez: use Evals: pin baseline, run your test-set on new variants, Console compares structured-output diffs and flags regression. You can gate rollouts based on eval pass rates.

[33:30] [35:00] Jamie Park: quick callout — competitors sometimes require heavy client-side logic to enforce schemas; Redwood centralizes enforcement and gives traceability and repair tools out of the box, which speeds up production readiness.
[34:20] Priya Singh: do you support SCIM provisioning for RBAC?
[34:35] Luis Ramirez: yes SCIM + SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC for Console resources.
[35:45] Tom Reynolds: any limits on schema size or complexity?

[36:00] Luis Ramirez: practical limits: very large schemas increase validation latency; we suggest schema payloads under a few KB for low latency paths; for complex objects consider staged validation or a two-call approach.
[36:40] Aisha Khan: can we run the POC in our cloud region (eu-west-1)?
[36:55] Jamie Park: yes, Dedicated and Private can be region-pinned; Hosted has multi-region endpoints and we can ensure data residency via region scoping on the account.

[37:30] [39:00] Luis Ramirez: final demo piece: function-calling plus tool-chaining — model creates an order, order service applies business rules, then a notification tool is called. You can see the entire chain in the trace and the per-call latency.
[38:20] Tom Reynolds: can we redact PII from traces before it hits your storage?
[38:35] Luis Ramirez: yes, you can configure auto-redaction at the route level and also set Console to send only metadata to Redwood while full payloads go to your S3.
[39:10] Aisha Khan: ok great, summarizes for next steps?

[39:25] Jamie Park: recap — we'll send POC outline and pricing, Luis will share benchmark template and sample schemas, Priya will send security checklist, target kickoff week of 2027-02-14. Pricing and security pack due end of week.
[40:05] Aisha Khan: sounds good. One last thing — can you include an example of the repaired JSON in the follow-up email?
[40:20] Luis Ramirez: yes we'll include the before/after payloads and the Console trace snippet. Also attach sample code for both API request and registering a tool endpoint.
[41:00] [42:00] Tom Reynolds: small nit — our infra team needs the exact header/mTLS handshake sequence for Private, can you put that in the runbook?
[41:15] Jamie Park: will do, Luis will add the handshake details and sample config.
[41:45] Priya Singh: also please include the data retention matrix and steps for cert rotation.
[42:05] Jamie Park: included in the security pack we'll send.
[42:40] [45:00] Luis Ramirez: final Q&A — any blockers we should know about before the POC?
[42:55] Aisha Khan: main blockers: internal stakeholder alignment and timing; security alignment seems ok if we get the docs. Cost is a second check but we expect to scope it.
[43:30] Jamie Park: understood. We'll keep the POC scoped and lightweight and show measurable results quickly.
[44:00] Aisha Khan: thanks all, appreciate the demo. Looking forward to the POC details.
[44:12] Jamie Park: thanks everyone. We'll follow up with notes, the POC sheet, security pack, and benchmark spreadsheet. Meeting adjourned.
End of transcript.
